Multi-negative sampled softmax is a well-supported first experiment within NextItNet: the original [NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf) explicitly supports sampled-softmax training. [Wu et al., TOIS 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) show that sampled softmax emphasizes high-scoring negatives through larger gradients and connects optimization to DCG; their empirical evidence concerns collaborative-filtering models, so it does not establish gains for NextItNet or Electronics. Explicit mining adds another choice: [GNNO, SIGIR 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10047) constructs an item-transition graph from training sequences and uses neighborhood overlap with an easy-to-hard curriculum, reporting improvements on three Amazon benchmarks.

Hardest negatives can also be unobserved positives. [Hard-BPR, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) modifies the ranking objective to reduce false-negative damage under dynamic hard sampling. [UFNRec, SDM 2023](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611977653.ch6) instead identifies potential false negatives and reverses their labels with EMA and consistency safeguards; inferred relevance remains uncertain. Practical hypothesis: compare uniform multi-negative softmax against a warm-started mixture of uniform and moderately hard negatives, optionally downweighting suspicious negatives using training-only evidence. This is an experimental proposal, not an established Electronics result. Keep one jointly trained NextItNet per category, exclude observed training positives from negative pools, and never consult held-out labels for filtering. Select using unchanged host validation candidates and macro HR@10; larger sampled margins alone do not demonstrate generalization.
